name: Validating Manufacturing AI
blurb: Credibility and validation for AI that supports quality decisions.
title: Validating Manufacturing AI
answer: When an AI model supports a quality decision, the FDA's draft credibility framework and GMP validation both apply. ISPE's GAMP guide on AI translates this into practice for computerised systems, with emphasis on data, testing and change control.

reading.body:
Manufacturing AI that supports a quality decision must satisfy two frameworks at once: the FDA's draft credibility guidance and GMP computerised system validation. ISPE's GAMP guide on AI is the document that translates both into practice.

The two frameworks answer different questions. GAMP covers the established ground of requirements, risk assessment, supplier assessment, configuration control, testing and documentation. The FDA credibility framework addresses how much evidence is enough, scaled to how much the decision rests on the model and how serious a wrong decision would be. The AI-specific additions sit on top of the GAMP base: fitness of training data, independent test data, predefined performance criteria, explainability where needed, and monitoring after release.

Responsibility does not transfer with the software. A vendor can supply documentation and testing, but the manufacturer remains responsible for validating the system in its intended use. That matters for AI specifically because model behaviour can drift after release, so validation is not a one-time gate. The stated payoff is that one approach built on GAMP and the FDA framework can serve both US and EU inspections, letting a global manufacturer run the same process across sites.

The data covers two developments, the FDA draft guidance in January 2025 and the ISPE GAMP Guide: Artificial Intelligence in 2025, and it does not say whether either has been finalised. It names draft Annex 22 as a third reference point without describing its contents. It also does not quantify how much validation effort any particular model requires, which is the question a manufacturing team will actually face.

explainer:
Validating manufacturing AI combines established computerised system validation with AI specific checks. The established part covers requirements, risk assessment, supplier assessment, configuration control, testing and documentation, typically following GAMP. The AI specific part covers the fitness of training data, independent test data, predefined performance criteria, explainability where needed, and monitoring after release.

Where a model supports a quality decision, the FDA's draft credibility framework adds a structured way to decide how much evidence is enough, based on how much the decision rests on the model and how serious a wrong decision would be. Using one validation approach that satisfies GAMP, the FDA framework and draft Annex 22 lets a global manufacturer run the same process across sites.

Why ordinary validation does not quite fit

Computer system validation assumes software does the same thing every time and that a test performed once stays valid. A machine learning model does not fit that assumption. Its behaviour comes from data rather than from code a reviewer can read, it can give different outputs for inputs it has never seen, and it can be retrained, after which the old evidence no longer describes the new model. So validation has to add some things.

What gets added

First, a documented intended use and the operating range of inputs the model was built for, so that out of range inputs are detected rather than silently answered. Second, evidence of performance on held out data that represents real production, including the hard cases and the rare ones. Third, performance monitoring in use, with thresholds that trigger review. Fourth, a change control process that treats retraining as a change, with its own evidence, and that records every model version. Fifth, a defined human role: what the person checks, how often, and what they can override.

What regulators have said

Agencies have published principles for AI in drug manufacturing and in devices that point the same way: risk based, lifecycle focused, with the depth of evidence matched to the model's influence on quality. None of this requires novel science. It requires the plant to write down what it would do for a new instrument, apply it to a model, and keep the records current as the model changes.
